newsitem.title: USA: Dade County, Fla., seeks list of bond firm probes.
newsitem.headline: Dade County, Fla., seeks list of bond firm probes.

text.p: The chairman of Dade County's finance committee called for "a good hard look" at the way the county selects bond participants and said he would ask all the firms Dade uses for a report listing allegations and investigations involving their companies.
"There has been a tremendous spotlight on the financial activity of this community," Commissioner Jimmy Morales said. "It merits a good hard look."

Morales, who chairs the commission's finance and trust funds committee, said he would ask all the county's underwriters, bond counsel and financial advisers to report "where they stand in terms of investigations, allegations and so forth."
He said he would ask for the reports at the committee's January meeting. A date has not been scheduled.
Morales made the remarks during a discussion of whether Howard Gary & Co and Grigsby & Co should be allowed to participate in Dade issues.

The Miami Herald has reported that federal investigators recorded a converstation in which firm owners Howard Gary and Calvin Grigsby discussed an alleged kickback with Dade County Commissioner James Burke in connection with a Dade bond issue.

None of them have been charged, and the U.S. Justice Department gave assurances that Howard Gary & Co is not the target of its ongoing investigation into allegations of corruption in City of Miami and Dade County bond deals.
Gary's lawyer has said Gary acted as an informant for the federal government.
Gary's firm was subsequently removed as senior manager on a Dade County seaport bond issue amid concerns the allegations would affect disclosure and pricing.

But the firm was allowed to act as co-manager on a $120 million solid waste refunding issue by the county earlier this month, and has been assigned as co-manager to Dade's $450 million water and sewer revenue bond issue, scheduled for pricing January 8 and 9.
Both Howard Gary & Co and Grigsby & Co remain in the county's underwriter pool, though Grigsby & Co is not presently assigned to any Dade deals.
"I would welcome a temporary suspension of both of these companies from serving on the underwriting team," Morales said.
He did not offer a formal resolution to that effect, but said he would ask the full 13-member commission to suspend them at a commission meeting next week.

Commissioners Katy Sorenson and Barbara Carey questioned whether it was fair to suspend them when they had not been charged with wrong doing. County officials said Gary's participation had no impact on pricing in the solid waste deal.
Grigsby vice president Lourdes Reyes said in a letter to the committee that the firm remains viable and that "As you can imagine, it is impossible to defend yourselves against newspaper articles."
Gary's attorney, Peter Raben, said suspending the firms would violate their right to due process.
"The law does not permit sanctions, punishment, disentitlement based on newspaper reports or newspaper allegations," Raben said.

Gary said several other firms that do business with the county have been the subject of federal and regulatory investigations, fines and charges but were allowed to remain in Dade's underwriting pool.
"Why are we being treated differently?" Gary asked.

At that point, Morales said he would ask for an accounting from all the firms. He said he would also consult with other large cities, bond rating agencies and industry officials to determine whether Dade's system of choosing bond issue participants is fair and efficient.
"There are no sacred cows. Everything needs to be looked at fresh, brand new," the newly elected commissioner said.

Dade uses three firms as financial adivsers and has standing pools of 20 underwriters and 16 bond counsel firms chosen through RFPs. In the underwriting pool, there are standing teams whose members act as senior manager on a rotating basis, although exceptions are sometimes made when conflicts arise.
